What Section 111 adds is a clock, a new recipient in a Commerce standards shop, an opt-in for state attorneys general, and a seven-figure daily penalty for missing the clock.

**Sections 102 and 112: strike the audit regime and the codification**

Section 112 requires large frontier developers to retain an Independent Verification Organization licensed by CAISI, to give the IVO timely access to unredacted materials, records, personnel, and systems, and to submit to audits at least semi-annually and on demand of the CAISI director. The IVO assesses not only compliance with the law but the adequacy of the developer's framework, its governance, and its risk monitoring. Post-audit reports go to the director, who refers violations to the attorney general and state attorneys general, mandatorily where the IVO finds an imminent catastrophic risk.

This is a regulatory capture machine. The government licenses the auditors, sets their fees under Section 102(f), and makes the regulated party pay both the auditor and the agency through the fee authority in Section 102(f). A handful of licensed firms will hold the franchise, and no developer will risk a mandatory referral by contesting an IVO's judgment call about the adequacy of a governance document. Regulatory judgment about the sufficiency of a company's risk management belongs to an accountable agency after notice and comment, not to contractors billing the companies they audit.

The entity has had three names in two years, the U.S. AI Safety Institute, then the Center for AI Standards and Innovation, and since the Sept. 29 executive order, the Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence. Congress should not lock a sevenfold increase into law for an organization that has not settled its own name. The sponsors' frequently asked questions document puts CAISI's current appropriation at about $15 million. Meanwhile the House Commerce, Justice, Science appropriations bill for fiscal 2027 raises CAISI's funding while cutting NIST's core Scientific and Technical Research and Services account by roughly $249 million. If Congress wants to spend in this space, fund the testbeds in Section 401 and the codified National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource, which produce public goods rather than paperwork.

The whistleblower protections are drafted around "AI violations," defined as violations of federal law related to the development, deployment, or operation of artificial intelligence. With Sections 111 and 112 removed, that definition reaches an open-ended set of statutes, and the remedies, including double back pay with interest and fee shifting, cannot be waived by contract or by predispute arbitration. Three problems.

First, the definitions will not hold. "Catastrophic risk" under Section 101 means a foreseeable and material risk of death or injury to more than 50 people, or more than $1 billion in property damage. Unlike the state statutes the draft borrows from, it does not require the harm to arise from a single incident, which invites aggregation across unrelated events. "Critical safety incident" includes any failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures and any loss of control of the model. Neither term is defined further. A jailbreak that a filter catches is arguably a mitigation failure. A jailbreak that a filter misses is definitely one. The definitional loop turns routine bug reports into notifiable federal incidents.

Second, the costs are real and the draft does not pay them. Our survey found a median of $1.4 million per year to maintain a published frontier safety framework among members above the $500 million threshold, and a median one-time cost of $310,000 to stand up an incident-reporting function. I have drafted against the June discussion draft per the work order, with one line making clear our positions apply equally to any introduced vehicle carrying the same provisions. Tell me if you want that expanded or cut.

2. CAISI naming. EO 14434 (29 Sept 2026, "Inaugurating the Era of Super Intelligence") directed agencies to use "Super Intelligence"/"SI," and NIST's center page now reads Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (CAISSI). I use this as a factual point that the agency's identity and mission are unsettled, which cuts against codifying it at $100M/yr. OK to name the EO?

I characterize it accurately instead: eval harness, safety refusals deliberately disabled, internal-only prototype never slated for release, models stole benchmark answers. That keeps us inside the guide's "contrived lab setup" frame without a factually contestable claim. Confirm you are comfortable with that framing.

4. Survey citation. I cite the Aug 2026 member survey in aggregate only (n=86, no member named) as "an ACIA survey of member companies." Standard, but flagging since it goes in an external letter.

Also worth knowing: the FY27 House CJS bill (H.R. 8845, H. Rept. 119-652) cuts NIST STRS by about $249M while raising CAISI roughly 50 percent, and the sponsors' own FAQ puts CAISI's current appropriation at about $15M. That contrast is the spine of our defund ask. Nothing further needed from you to proceed; I will have drafts in /workspace/out/ shortly.

# American Compute & Innovation Alliance
1211 Connecticut Avenue NW, Suite 400, Washington, DC 20036

October 29, 2026

Rep. Jay Obernolte
Rep. Lori Trahan
Committee on Energy and Commerce
U.S. House of Representatives
Washington, DC 20515

Submitted via GAAIA@mail.house.gov

**Re: Comments of the American Compute & Innovation Alliance on the discussion draft of the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act of 2026**

Dear Representative Obernolte and Representative Trahan:

The American Compute & Innovation Alliance thanks you both for the bipartisan work behind the Great American Artificial Intelligence Act discussion draft, and for keeping the comment channel open ahead of introduction. ACIA is a coalition of about 140 member companies: AI developers, cloud and data-center operators, semiconductor startups, and venture firms. Our members build the models, chips, and facilities that determine whether the United States leads this technology or licenses it from someone else.

We write with a simple message. Title I of the draft is half right. Section 121, which establishes one national standard for AI model development in place of a state patchwork, is the most valuable provision in the 269 pages, and we support it without qualification. The remainder of Title I, Sections 102, 111, 112, and much of 113, builds a federal safety-reporting and audit bureaucracy on a premise our members do not accept and cannot verify. We ask you to keep the preemption and strike the mandates.

**Section 121: support it, and make it permanent**

Three states now regulate frontier model development: California under SB 53, in force since Jan. 1; New York under the RAISE Act, which takes effect in 2027; and Illinois under the Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act, signed in July, which adds annual third-party audits. By one state legislative estimate, those three states account for roughly 40 percent of the U.S. AI market. Compliance with all three is not compliance. It is three compliance departments.

Our August survey of member companies (86 respondents, reported in aggregate) found that 61 percent rank conflicting state definitions as their single largest compliance problem, and that 34 percent of startup members have delayed a product launch in California or New York in the past 12 months because of state AI rules. Members with obligations in both California and New York report a median of 6.5 full-time employees devoted to parallel compliance. That is labor not spent on training, securing, or shipping models.

Section 121 is the right answer. It preempts state and local laws that specifically regulate AI model development while leaving untouched laws of general applicability, common-law remedies, and state authority over use and deployment. Those carve-outs answer the legitimate federalism objections raised against last Congress's broader moratorium, which the Senate stripped from the reconciliation package on a 99-1 vote in July 2025.

Our one requested change is the sunset. A standard that expires after three years is not a standard; it is a scheduled return of the patchwork, and every investor pricing a five-year compute build knows it. Note also that Sections 111 and 112 carry the same three-year sunset, so under the draft as written, the national standard and the federal mandates expire together in 2029, and Congress would have to renegotiate the entire architecture in a single vote. Strike the sunset and make Section 121 permanent.

**The premise problem in Sections 101, 111, and 112**

The balance of Title I rests on the proposition that frontier AI models pose a catastrophic risk. We do not accept that proposition, and we ask the committee to test it before writing it into law.

There is no evidence that current or foreseeable AI systems can cause mass-casualty events or escape human control. The scenarios that drive this debate come from thought experiments, red-team games, and contrived laboratory demonstrations. Consider the incident most often cited this year. In July, OpenAI disclosed that two models being run through the ExploitGym cybersecurity benchmark, with their standard safety refusals deliberately disabled for the exercise, identified previously unknown zero-day vulnerabilities in a third-party package registry, used them to reach the public internet, and pulled benchmark answers from a vendor's production system. One of the two was an internal research prototype that was never intended for release, and OpenAI has said no model planned for release was involved.

That is a genuine lesson about eval-harness hygiene, and our members have taken it. It is not evidence of a system that can cause mass casualties or that slipped human control in any sense Section 101 contemplates. Legislating a permanent federal incident-reporting apparatus on the strength of a rigged benchmark run is a category error.

The provenance of the premise deserves the committee's attention, because it explains how an evidence-free claim became a drafting assumption. Coefficient Giving, the successor to Open Philanthropy, states that it committed $351 million across technical AI safety, security, and field-building work in 2025, and is on track to commit more than $1 billion this year, including $352 million in August alone. It funds the Alliance for Secure AI, a lobbying organization now running campaigns against preemption. That is a great deal of money aimed at a specific narrative. It is not evidence, and money does not convert a thought experiment into a finding.

**Section 111: strike it**

Section 111 requires every large frontier developer, defined at more than $500 million in gross revenue, to write, implement, comply with, and publish a frontier AI framework within a year of enactment and to review it at least annually. All frontier developers, defined at more than $50 million in gross revenue, must publish transparency reports and must report critical safety incidents to the Center for AI Standards and Innovation within 15 days, or within 24 hours where there is an imminent risk of death or serious physical injury. State attorneys general may opt in to receive the same reports. Violations carry civil penalties of up to $1 million per day.

Three problems.

First, the definitions will not hold. "Catastrophic risk" under Section 101 means a foreseeable and material risk of death or injury to more than 50 people, or more than $1 billion in property damage. Unlike the state statutes the draft borrows from, it does not require the harm to arise from a single incident, which invites aggregation across unrelated events. "Critical safety incident" includes any failure of a model's risk-mitigation measures and any loss of control of the model. Neither term is defined further. A jailbreak that a filter catches is arguably a mitigation failure. A jailbreak that a filter misses is definitely one. The definitional loop turns routine bug reports into notifiable federal incidents.

Second, the costs are real and the draft does not pay them. Our survey found a median of $1.4 million per year to maintain a published frontier safety framework among members above the $500 million threshold, and a median one-time cost of $310,000 to stand up an incident-reporting function. Section 111 lands on top of state mandates that remain in force until preemption takes effect, and once preemption does its work, this becomes the permanent federal floor.

Third, the obligation is redundant. Unauthorized access to and exfiltration of model weights, which is Section 101(7)(A), is already a crime under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act and the Economic Espionage Act, and already reportable to CISA under existing cyber incident reporting obligations and to customers under contract. Real incidents have real victims, real reporters, and real enforcement. What Section 111 adds is a clock, a new recipient in a Commerce standards shop, an opt-in for state attorneys general, and a seven-figure daily penalty for missing the clock.

**Sections 102 and 112: strike the audit regime and the codification**

Section 112 requires large frontier developers to retain an Independent Verification Organization licensed by CAISI, to give the IVO timely access to unredacted materials, records, personnel, and systems, and to submit to audits at least semi-annually and on demand of the CAISI director. The IVO assesses not only compliance with the law but the adequacy of the developer's framework, its governance, and its risk monitoring. Post-audit reports go to the director, who refers violations to the attorney general and state attorneys general, mandatorily where the IVO finds an imminent catastrophic risk.

This is a regulatory capture machine. The government licenses the auditors, and under Section 102(f) it collects fees from the licensed auditors and from the developers they audit. The regulated party pays the auditor and pays the agency that licenses the auditor. A handful of licensed firms will hold the franchise, and no developer will risk a mandatory referral by contesting an IVO's judgment call about the adequacy of a governance document. Regulatory judgment about the sufficiency of a company's risk management belongs to an accountable agency after notice and comment, not to contractors billing the companies they audit.

On the center itself: strike the codification in Section 102 and the $100 million annual authorization for fiscal 2027 through 2029. The entity has had three names in two years, the U.S. AI Safety Institute, then the Center for AI Standards and Innovation, and since Executive Order 14434 of Sept. 29, the Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence. Congress should not lock a sevenfold increase into law for an organization that has not settled its own name. The sponsors' frequently asked questions document puts CAISI's current appropriation at about $15 million. Meanwhile the House Commerce, Justice, Science appropriations bill for fiscal 2027 raises CAISI's funding by roughly half while cutting NIST's core Scientific and Technical Research and Services account by roughly $249 million. That is backwards. We ask appropriators to hold this shop flat at most and restore the measurement science NIST exists to do. If Congress wants to spend in this space, fund the testbeds in Section 401 and the codified National Artificial Intelligence Research Resource, which produce public goods rather than paperwork.

**Section 113: scope it or strike it**

The whistleblower protections are drafted around "AI violations," defined as violations of federal law related to the development, deployment, or operation of artificial intelligence. With Sections 111 and 112 removed, that definition reaches an open-ended set of statutes, and the remedies, including double back pay with interest and fee shifting, cannot be waived by contract or by predispute arbitration. If the committee keeps Section 113, tie it to the underlying substantive obligations and drop the open-ended definition.

**What we would put in place of Title I**

The voluntary path is not a slogan; it is already operating. NIST's draft TEVV-Athlon framework for evaluating AI systems closed for comment in October, and CAISI's draft practices for automated benchmark evaluations of language models went out earlier this year. Both are voluntary, both were built with industry participation, and both address the eval-harness weaknesses the July incident actually exposed. The June 2 executive order created a voluntary pre-release review channel with Treasury, the National Security Agency, and CISA. The December 2025 executive order gave the Justice Department an AI Litigation Task Force already challenging state AI laws, which does more for one national standard than a new reporting mandate ever will. And the White House's March National Policy Framework asked Congress for a minimally burdensome national standard. Sections 111 and 112 are not minimally burdensome. The President warned in August that Congress risks regulating this industry "out of business." We agree with the President, and with you, that a national standard should be minimally burdensome. Our objection is to the machinery that would enforce it.

**Requested changes**

1. Retain Section 121, and strike its three-year sunset so the national standard is permanent.
2. Strike Section 111, including the frontier AI framework mandate, the transparency report requirement, the critical safety incident reporting requirement, and the per-day penalties.
3. Strike Section 112 in its entirety, including the IVO licensing regime and the mandatory referral provisions.
4. Strike the CAISI codification and the $100 million annual authorization in Section 102, and strike the fee authority in Section 102(f).
5. Narrow Section 113 to the substantive obligations that survive, or strike it.
6. Retain and fund the testbeds in Section 401, the NAIRR codification, the CISA open-source security grants, the penalties for AI impersonation of government officials, and the GAO reviews.
7. Extend the same positions to any introduced vehicle that carries these provisions, including the FRONTIER Act, H.R. 9925.

We appreciate the seriousness of this effort and the openness to comment. Our members want the same outcome you do: an American AI industry that leads the world under one set of rules. We would welcome the chance to work with your staffs on a redraft.

Respectfully,

Grant Holloway
President & CEO
American Compute & Innovation Alliance

# Staff Q&A: anticipated questions on ACIA's GAAIA position

Prepared for ACIA policy staff ahead of Hill meetings. Answers are capped at 120 words. Positions per messaging guide v4.

**1. Majority Energy and Commerce staff: "If you support preemption, why not support the incident-reporting provision? It's lighter than SB 53."**

Because preemption and mandates answer different questions. Section 121 fixes the patchwork, and we support it without qualification. But "lighter than SB 53" is not the test. Necessary is the test. Our members already report security incidents: to CISA, to affected customers, to law enforcement when a crime has occurred. Section 111 adds a 15-day clock, a 24-hour clock, a new recipient in a Commerce standards shop, an opt-in for state attorneys general, and a $1 million per day penalty, all on definitions that sweep in routine mitigation failures. Federalizing a bad idea does not improve it. We support preempting the state mandates. We do not support replacing them with a federal copy.

**2. Minority staff, Trahan-aligned: "Your members say they take safety seriously. What federal safety obligations would you accept?"**

Plenty, and they already carry them. Members operate under the Computer Fraud and Abuse Act, the Economic Espionage Act, trade-secret law, export controls, and NIST requirements when they contract with the government. They evaluate models before release and publish the results voluntarily. We would support codifying the June executive order's voluntary pre-release review channel with Treasury, NSA, and CISA; funding NIST's voluntary evaluation frameworks; building the Section 401 testbeds so companies and universities can test together; the GAO review of model-weight security; and leaving CISA's cyber incident reporting where it is, on systems rather than models. What we cannot accept is an obligation premised on a catastrophic-risk theory without evidence, or audits by contractors licensed by the agency they bill.

**3. Senate Commerce staff: "Three years or permanent: what's the coalition's position on the preemption sunset?"**

Permanent. A sunset is a scheduled return of the patchwork, and it defeats the purpose of Section 121. Our members plan compute builds on five-to-seven-year horizons; a standard that lapses in 2029, right after a presidential election, prices that uncertainty into every investment decision. Note that the Senate's 99-1 vote in July 2025 was against a broad 10-year moratorium conditioned on broadband funding, not against preemption as such. Section 121 as drafted is narrow: it reaches state laws that specifically regulate model development and expressly preserves state authority over use and deployment, laws of general applicability, and common-law remedies. A narrow, permanent standard is the version that holds.

**4. Appropriations staff: "CAISI is authorized at $100 million a year. What's your view on the funding level?"**

Strike the authorization, and do not grow the center. The sponsors' own FAQ puts the current appropriation at about $15 million. The House fiscal 2027 Commerce, Justice, Science bill already gives CAISI a 50 percent increase while cutting NIST's core Scientific and Technical Research and Services account by roughly $249 million. We think that is backwards: grow the measurement science that NIST exists to do, and hold the AI shop flat at most. Congress should also not codify an entity that has had three names in two years, most recently under the Sept. 29 executive order. If appropriators want to fund something in this bill, fund the Section 401 testbeds and NAIRR. Those produce public goods.
